subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Reference Price Manipulation
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Reference Price Manipulation.

hook.text: A tag reads: was $200, now $99. You feel you saved $101. The item was never sold at $200. The reference was invented.

buildup.text: Reference prices set expectations. A sale discount feels valuable only compared to a higher original price, real.

discovery.text: Retailers inflate original prices before sales events. The discount is measured from a phantom price nobody ever paid.

twist.text: JCPenney tried honest pricing: no fake sales, fair prices. Sales dropped 25%. Customers missed the thrill of a deal.

climax.text: Ignoring the was-price changes your shopping. Ask: would I buy this at this price without a sale sign?

punchline.text: The sale price is the real price. The original was the lie.

quiz.question: What happened when JCPenney eliminated fake sales and offered honest pricing?
options: Sales increased because customers trusted the company
Sales dropped 25% because customers missed the thrill of deals
There was no change in customer behavior

details.summary: Reference price manipulation inflates the perceived original price so that the sale price seems like a dramatic discount. A jacket marked down from 200 to 100 dollars feels like stealing, even if the jacket was never actually sold at 200 dollars.
details.whyItMatters: Retailers routinely inflate reference prices to create the illusion of savings. This practice exploits anchoring bias and the transaction utility people derive from feeling they got a deal, regardless of the item's true market value.
takeaways: Inflated original prices make discounts seem larger than they are
Transaction utility makes deals feel valuable independent of the item's worth
Regulators increasingly target deceptive reference pricing practices

faq.question: How do retailers inflate reference prices?
faq.answer: By initially listing products at prices they never intend to sell at, keeping them at the high price briefly before a perpetual sale, or comparing to manufacturer suggested retail prices that no retailer actually charges.

faq.question: Is reference price manipulation illegal?
faq.answer: In many jurisdictions, yes. Laws require the original price to reflect a genuine previous selling price maintained for a minimum period. However, enforcement is inconsistent and creative practices often skirt the rules.
